analysis.one_liner: Requires the federal minimum wage to cover a family of four's cost of living.
analysis.headline: The bill was never acted on: it died in committee with zero cosponsors after the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the federal minimum wage so that full-time pay had to cover housing, food, childcare, transportation, and healthcare for a family of four at the local cost of living. It would have added annual inflation adjustments and required federal and contract workers' wages to rise whenever Congress raises its own pay. It would also have extended the federal minimum wage to the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits: Full-time low-wage workers, especially federal and contractor employees earning poverty-level wages, who would see their pay set to actual local living costs rather than the national minimum wage floor

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require employers to pay a full-time worker enough to cover housing, food, childcare, transportation, and healthcare for a family of four, based on regional or municipal cost-of-living standards rather than the existing $5.15 national minimum wage [S2][S3].

It would add an annual cost-of-living adjustment so the wage floor tracks inflation, and would require federal and contract workers' wages to increase by the same percentage as congressional pay raises whenever Congress raises its own pay beyond the standard adjustment [S2][S3].

It would apply the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, which was then exempt, and require any product labeled 'Made in the USA' to be made at wages meeting the federal standard [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers paying below the new living-wage level, with federal contractors — a majority of them large defense contractors — bearing the largest cost increases; consumers would face some price increases as employers passed costs along

drawbacks.text: Binding wages to a regional family-of-four living cost would set the floor far above the then-current minimum, and employers could respond by cutting hours, raising prices, or reducing low-wage jobs; the bill includes no study or phase-in beyond a 60-day effective date [S3].

The mandate is administratively complex: the Labor Secretary would have to set locality-specific living-cost levels and fringe-benefit add-ons, which could be difficult to compute and litigate [S2][S3].

Applying the full standard to the Northern Mariana Islands immediately, with only a 60-day effective date, could impose a sudden, steep wage shock on that economy's garment and service industries [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: it directly attacks working poverty, and its findings cite data showing over a quarter of a million direct federal workers earning poverty wages and congressional pay rising 23% since the last minimum wage vote [S3]. But the bill was written as an aspiration, not a workable law: no cost analysis, a 60-day jump to a family-of-four living wage nationwide, and heavy administrative discretion. It attracted no cosponsors, which suggests even sympathetic colleagues doubted its design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never considered it, and the Congress ended three weeks later.

narrative.text: Cynthia McKinney introduced the bill on December 8, 2006, in the final weeks of the 109th Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day and received no hearing, markup, or floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers paying poverty-level wages — including large defense contractors and the Northern Mariana Islands garment industry — kept the status quo wage floor, while low-wage federal and contract workers gained nothing.

for.name: Cynthia McKinney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was her sole sponsorship and drew no cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Boehner (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan breakdown exists; the sponsor was a Democrat and the Republican-run committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill's findings state that 62% of federal contractors paying poverty-level wages are defense contractors and that most are large businesses [S3]. A living-wage mandate would directly raise their labor costs; their interest in keeping the wage floor low runs against the workers it would lift.

The bill would replace a $5.15 national floor with a locality-based family-of-four living wage, sharply raising labor costs for businesses that rely on minimum-wage workers [S2][S3]. Their cost-saving interest runs against the workers' need for a livable wage.

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands garment and light manufacturing
industries.note: The islands were then exempt from the federal minimum wage, allowing low-cost garment production, some of it labeled 'Made in the USA' [S3]. Extending the federal standard to the islands would end that cost advantage.
